Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models

Abstract

Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.11 1 We release our code at: https://github.com/wastedelement/pixel-model-analysis.

${\dagger}$${\dagger}$footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Pixel-based language models offer an alternative to subword tokenization by processing text as rendered images (Rust et al., 2023; Chai et al., 2024b; Kesen et al., 2025). Instead of mapping words to entries in a fixed vocabulary, they encode image patches containing the written text (Rust et al., 2023). This approach is particularly appealing for noisy and multilingual inputs: a typo can break a familiar word into unfamiliar subwords, while languages and scripts poorly covered by a tokenizer may receive uninformative representations. Rendering text avoids dependence on a learned subword vocabulary, motivating research on visual language representations, rendering strategies, and multilingual pixel-based language models (Lotz et al., 2023; Salesky et al., 2023; Kesen et al., 2025).

The promise of pixel-based language models depends on more than their accuracy on clean benchmarks. Before their robustness or multilingual coverage can be useful, their pretrained encoders must be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. Fine-tuning is therefore central to evaluating their practical value. Text-based models such as BERT learn contextual language representations by predicting masked tokens (Devlin et al., 2019), whereas pixel-based encoders reconstruct masked image patches (Rust et al., 2023). Although visual reconstruction also supports linguistic learning, existing probes suggest that semantic information is less readily accessible in the resulting representations than in BERT’s (Tatariya et al., 2024). This raises important questions of how much downstream adaptation pixel-based representations require and what allows this adaptation to succeed.

At the same time, the visual interface may provide distinct advantages once fine-tuning succeeds. Typographical errors often alter only local visual features while preserving the broader input structure. Similarly, rendering allows models to process new languages without depending on coverage from a fixed subword vocabulary. Pixel-based models may therefore be harder to adapt, yet more resilient when applied beyond clean English inputs. We investigate both sides of this trade-off.

To this end, we systematically compare pixel-based and text-based language models across downstream adaptation, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer (Figure 1). We first examine learning-rate sensitivity, fine-tuning duration, and labelled-data requirements, and then investigate whether pretrained representations contribute to adaptation difficulty. Finally, we evaluate successfully fine-tuned models under typographical noise and on languages unseen during downstream training. The key findings are as follows:

  • •

    Pixel-based models require more downstream adaptation (§4). They require more careful optimization, longer training, and broader labelled-data coverage, while task-relevant information appears less readily accessible in their pretrained representations.

  • •

    Pixel-based models show strong resilience to typographical errors (§5). Successfully fine-tuned models retain more of their performance as noise increases and can outperform text-based counterparts under heavy noise.

  • •

    Pixel-based models support effective zero-shot crosslingual transfer (§6). After English fine-tuning, they achieve higher average target-language performance than the text-based counterparts on two benchmarks.

2 Related Work

2.1 Pixel-Based Language Models

Most language models tokenize text using fixed subword vocabularies, with approaches like BPE (Sennrich et al., 2016), WordPiece (Devlin et al., 2019; Song et al., 2021), and SentencePiece (Kudo, 2018; Kudo and Richardson, 2018). Tokenizer-free language models offer an alternative by processing text directly as characters or bytes (Clark et al., 2022; Xue et al., 2022). Further work reduces computational cost by grouping characters or bytes into variable-length units, using learned boundaries or input-dependent segmentation (Godey et al., 2022; Nawrot et al., 2023; Pagnoni et al., 2025).

Pixel-based language models take a visual approach, encoding rendered text as image patches (Rust et al., 2023). Research in this direction has explored rendering strategies (Lotz et al., 2023), autoregressive pretraining (Chai et al., 2024b; Tai et al., 2024), and multilingual representations (Salesky et al., 2023; Kesen et al., 2025). Linguistic probing further examines what these visual representations learn about language (Tatariya et al., 2024). Alongside these developments, studies of text-based models have seen substantial variation in fine-tuning outcomes (Dodge et al., 2020; Mosbach et al., 2021; Liu and Wang, 2021). We bring these questions together by examining how reliably pixel-based models learn downstream tasks, how much supervision they require, and how their pretrained representations support adaptation.

2.2 Robustness and Crosslingual Transfer

Typographical robustness concerns whether models preserve their predictions when small changes alter the written form of an input. Character-level attacks and misspellings can substantially degrade NLP systems, motivating methods for robust text processing (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Pruthi et al., 2019; Moradi and Samwald, 2021). Byte-level and visual representations have shown resilience to such perturbations (Xue et al., 2022; Salesky et al., 2021; Rust et al., 2023). Recent work introduces more realistic, language-specific typing errors (Zhao et al., 2026). We build on this work by comparing pixel-based and text-based models under typographical noise, examining both clean accuracy and degradation as noise increases.

Crosslingual transfer enables models to apply knowledge learned in one source language to tasks in other target languages, reducing the need for labelled data in each language (Pires et al., 2019; Dufter and Schütze, 2020; Conneau et al., 2020b; Lauscher et al., 2020; Ruder et al., 2021; de Vries et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a). Visual text representations have also been shown to boost crosslingual transfer through shared visual patterns, especially for translation and language understanding (Salesky et al., 2023; Kesen et al., 2025). Building on this work, we examine how well pixel-based models transfer the task knowledge acquired during source-language fine-tuning to other languages.

3 General Experimental Setup

3.1 Models

Pixel-based models.

Our primary pixel-based model is PIXEL-base, pretrained through masked autoencoding on rendered English Wikipedia and BookCorpus (Rust et al., 2023). We also include English PIXEL-bigrams and the smaller PIXEL-tiny-continuous to examine models with different rendering schemes and capacities. For multilingual pretraining, we include PIXEL-M4, which uses bigram rendering and is pretrained on English, Hindi, Ukrainian, and Chinese (Kesen et al., 2025).

Text-based models.

Our primary text-based model is BERT-base (Devlin et al., 2019), whose English pretraining sources broadly match those of PIXEL-base. This pair forms the main comparison throughout our analyses. We additionally include RoBERTa as a monolingual reference model (Liu et al., 2019), and mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019; Pires et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020a) as multilingual reference models.

3.2 Datasets

We evaluate models on tasks covering different aspects of language understanding, including sentiment analysis, grammatical acceptability, natural language inference, paraphrase identification, and topic classification. The datasets are introduced below, with more details presented in §B.

SST-2.

SST-2 is an English sentiment classification dataset with positive and negative labels for movie-review text (Socher et al., 2013).

MNLI.

MNLI is an English natural language inference dataset containing premise–hypothesis pairs from multiple genres, labelled as entailment, contradiction, or neutral (Williams et al., 2018).

CoLA.

CoLA is an English grammatical acceptability classification dataset containing sentences labelled as grammatically acceptable or unacceptable (Warstadt et al., 2019).

XNLI.

XNLI is a multilingual natural language inference benchmark with the same three-way classification task as MNLI (Conneau et al., 2018).

PAWS-X.

PAWS-X is a multilingual paraphrase identification dataset containing sentence pairs with high lexical overlap but potentially different meanings (Yang et al., 2019).

SIB-200.

SIB-200 is a multilingual sentence-level topic classification dataset derived from FLORES-200 (Team et al., 2022). The dataset is annotated with seven labels (Adelani et al., 2024).

Taxi1500.

Taxi1500 is a multilingual text classification dataset constructed from the Bible and annotated with six topics (Ma et al., 2025).

3.3 Fine-Tuning and Evaluation

We fine-tune pretrained models on labelled English data for each task. For each task, we initialize the encoder from a pretrained checkpoint, add a classification head, and fine-tune both components simultaneously.22 2 We also compare training from scratch and training only a classifier on a frozen pretrained encoder in §4.3. We select checkpoints based on English development performance and compare models on the same hold-out evaluation examples.

Our analyses examine both the adaptation process and the behavior of the fine-tuned models. For fine-tuning analysis, we study how training conditions and labelled data affect learning and the resulting representations (§4). For typographical robustness, we evaluate models trained on clean text on both clean inputs and their perturbed counterparts, without additional training on noisy data (§5). For zero-shot crosslingual transfer, we evaluate models fine-tuned on English on target-language inputs without target-language supervision (§6). Details are described in the corresponding sections.

4 Fine-Tuning Analysis

We examine what makes downstream adaptation challenging for pixel-based language models. Our analysis addresses three questions: (1) how optimization settings and training duration affect adaptation, (2) how labelled-data coverage affects generalization, and (3) whether the pretraining–adaptation gap contributes to fine-tuning instability. We primarily compare PIXEL-base and BERT-base on MNLI and SST-2 in this section.33 3 Further details and analyses, including renderer–checkpoint compatibility, are provided in §A.

4.1 Optimization and Fine-Tuning Duration

We compare the two models across six learning rates on a fixed subset of 24,000 MNLI examples, using ten random seeds per rate. Both models share the optimization settings and a ten-epoch observation window under the same learning-rate schedule. We assess training progress and evaluate development-selected checkpoints on separate holdout examples.44 4 The complete training recipe and per-seed results are given in §A.2 and §A.3; schedule follow-ups appear in §A.4. We additionally plot development accuracy at each epoch in recorded MNLI runs, using each model’s own training schedule. The results are demonstrated in Figure 2.

Pixel-based models are more sensitive to learning rate.

Within the same ten-epoch budget, BERT trains successfully across all ten seeds at every tested learning rate.55 5 We consider a run successful if its training loss is below 1.0 and its training accuracy exceeds 50% at epoch 10. For PIXEL, only eight or nine of the ten runs succeed at intermediate learning rates, and none succeed at the lowest or highest rates (Figure 2a). This sensitivity is particularly clear between 4×10−54\times 10^{-5} and 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}: this small increase reduces the number of successful runs from nine to zero and lowers mean held-out accuracy from 61.4% to 36.4% (Figure 2b). By comparison, BERT succeeds in every run and maintains approximately 77% accuracy at both rates. Thus, PIXEL has a narrower effective learning-rate range than BERT, and even rates within this range do not consistently produce successful training.

Pixel-based models can require longer fine-tuning.

The development curves show that PIXEL can begin learning substantially later than BERT (Figure 2c). In the illustrated MNLI runs, BERT reaches 76.2% development accuracy by epoch 2, whereas PIXEL remains between 33% and 38% throughout the first 10 epochs. PIXEL begins to improve sharply only after this point, reaching 55.7% at epoch 15 and 62.2% at epoch 25. Continuing beyond the first 10 epochs therefore yields a further 24.3-point improvement over its best accuracy within that initial window. This pattern also appears across multiple runs in our longer-budget analysis reported in Appendix A.7: among the seven seeds for which PIXEL trains successfully, its best checkpoint occurs at a median of 21 epochs, compared with only 3 epochs for BERT on the same seeds. A short fine-tuning schedule may therefore stop PIXEL before substantial learning begins, making a longer training window and greater patience necessary.

4.2 Supervision Budget

We examine how the amount of labelled data affects downstream performance while keeping the number of training updates fixed. We train both models on SST-2 subsets containing 2,000, 8,000, or 24,000 examples, and MNLI subsets containing 8,000 or 24,000 examples. Every run uses 15,000 updates with an effective batch size of 128. Each run therefore processes approximately the same total number of examples, but smaller training subsets are repeated more often. For the cross-budget comparison, we use three seeds per setting and report the best recorded development accuracy. 66 6 Subsets, model-specific learning rates, and complete results are detailed in Appendix A.5. The results are demonstrated in Figure 3.

Pixel-based models benefit more from additional labelled examples.

Under the same update budget, BERT gains only modestly from seeing more distinct training examples. Increasing the SST-2 training set from 2,000 to 8,000 examples improves its development accuracy by 2.0 points (Figure 3a), while increasing the MNLI training set from 8,000 to 24,000 examples produces a 3.8-point gain (Figure 3b). In comparison, PIXEL gains 12.0 points on SST-2 and 6.2 points on MNLI from the corresponding increases in labelled data. Because the number of training updates remains fixed (15,000 updates), these gains should be attributed to greater coverage of distinct labelled examples instead of additional optimization. Moreover, all runs finish with more than 99.5% online training accuracy, including those trained on the smallest subsets. Both models can therefore fit the available training data, but PIXEL relies more heavily on broader labelled-data coverage to generalize beyond it.77 7 Additional SST-2 experiments show that greater labelled data coverage does not eliminate variation and poor generalization across PIXEL runs. In a ten-seed experiment with 24,000 examples, all runs exceed 99.8% training accuracy, but two reach only 68.1–68.6% development accuracy, compared with 85.7–88.0% for the remaining runs; their test performance is similarly low. See Appendix A.5 for complete results.

4.3 Pretraining–Adaptation Gap

The preceding experiments show that PIXEL is harder to fine-tune than BERT and can fail under settings in which BERT trains reliably. This raises a further question: does pixel-based pretraining produce representations that require more adaptation before they can support downstream language tasks? We investigate this question through two complementary experiments.

First, we examine how much downstream performance is already supported by the pretrained representations (Figure 4a). We compare BERT-base and PIXEL-base on SST-2 under three different training conditions. In Random, the encoder and classifier are initialized randomly and trained jointly. In Frozen, the pretrained encoder remains fixed and only a linear classifier is trained on its mean-pooled representations. In Full FT, both the pretrained encoder and classifier are trained jointly. The comparison between Random and Full FT measures the value of pretrained initialization, while the comparison between Frozen and Full FT indicates how much the model benefits from adapting its pretrained representations to the task.

Second, we test whether previous supervised adaptation to another task makes subsequent MNLI fine-tuning more reliable (Figure 4b–c). Instead of initializing PIXEL from its original pretrained checkpoint, we use checkpoints previously fine-tuned on PAWS-X paraphrase identification or Taxi1500 topic classification. Neither task directly teaches MNLI-style inference, but both provide additional supervised training on sentence-level language understanding. If these checkpoints improve MNLI training, this would suggest that prior task adaptation provides PIXEL with a more suitable starting point for learning a new downstream task.

PIXEL requires substantially more downstream adaptation to become task-ready.

Pretraining benefits both models, but the gap between frozen representations and full fine-tuning is much larger for PIXEL. On SST-2, PIXEL reaches 54.0% accuracy from random initialization and 85.9% with full fine-tuning, showing a 31.9-point benefit from pretrained initialization (Figure 4a). However, training only a classifier on the frozen encoder reaches 66.7%, leaving a further 19.2-point improvement from adapting the encoder. For BERT, the corresponding accuracies are 78.8%, 86.1%, and 92.3% under Random, Frozen, and Full FT, respectively. Its frozen representations are therefore only 6.2 points behind full fine-tuning. While BERT’s pretrained representations already provide a strong basis for SST-2 classification, much of PIXEL’s downstream performance emerges only after its encoder is adapted. This suggests that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations.

Prior language-task adaptation provides PIXEL with a more reliable starting point.

We revisit two MNLI seeds that previously showed unstable training and rerun each seed five times from the original PIXEL checkpoint and from checkpoints adapted on PAWS-X or Taxi1500. For seed 100, the original checkpoint succeeds in only one of five runs, whereas both adapted checkpoints succeed in all five. For seed 5678, all five runs from the original checkpoint fail, while PAWS-X succeeds in all five runs and Taxi1500 in four (Figure 4b). The adapted checkpoints also begin learning earlier; by contrast, successful runs from the original checkpoint improve only after an initial plateau, while failed runs remain near chance accuracy (Figure 4c). Because PAWS-X and Taxi1500 involve different classification tasks, and their task-specific classifiers are discarded before MNLI fine-tuning, the improvement should be attributed to the change of encoders. The results therefore identify the pretrained encoder representation as an important contributor to PIXEL’s fine-tuning instability.

5 Typographical Robustness

The previous analysis examined the challenges of adapting pixel-based models to downstream tasks. We now ask whether, once successfully fine-tuned, these models are more robust to typographical errors (typos). Typos are common in user-written text (Conijn et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020) and can change how models tokenize and represent otherwise familiar words (Chai et al., 2024a). We examine both how typos affect input length and how well models maintain their task performance.

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate typographical robustness on SST-2 sentiment classification and MNLI natural language inference (Socher et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2018). Our primary comparison is between BERT-base and PIXEL-base. For each task, every model is fine-tuned on a fixed subset of 24,000 clean training examples, and checkpoints are selected based on clean development performance. The selected checkpoints are then evaluated, without further training, on clean evaluation examples and their typo-perturbed counterparts.88 8 Complete training and evaluation details, together with results for all models, are provided in §C. Additional CoLA fine-tuning results are reported in §A.8.

We generate the perturbed inputs using MulTypo, which simulates common typing mistakes through text-editing and keyboard-related operations (Zhao et al., 2026). We apply typo rates of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 40%, retain the original task labels, and present the same perturbed examples to every model. We measure performance degradation as the percentage of each model’s clean accuracy that is lost under noise. To examine how typos affect the input interface, we also report the percentage change in mean input length relative to clean inputs, measured in subword tokens for text-based models and image patches for pixel-based models. Figure 5 presents input-length change and relative accuracy loss for BERT-base and PIXEL-base, while Table 13 in the appendix reports absolute accuracy for all evaluated models.

5.2 Results and Discussion

Typos expand BERT’s token sequences but leave PIXEL’s patch sequences nearly unchanged.

BERT’s mean input length increases steadily with the typo rate, reaching 29.8% on SST-2 and 29.1% on MNLI at 40% noise (Figure 5a). By contrast, PIXEL-base’s mean patch length decreases by approximately 1% on both tasks, which is consistent with deletion operations slightly shortening the rendered text. These contrasting responses reflect how the two input interfaces handle misspellings. A typo can split a familiar word into multiple subword tokens, changing both the identities and positions of subsequent tokens. For PIXEL, the same typo changes local visual features but generally preserves the overall number of patches. The rendered interface therefore avoids the substantial sequence expansion observed with subword tokenization.

PIXEL-base retains more of its clean accuracy under typographical noise.

Across both tasks, BERT’s relative accuracy loss increases much more sharply than that of PIXEL-base (Figure 5b). At 40% noise, BERT loses 20.4% of its clean accuracy on SST-2 and 23.7% on MNLI, whereas PIXEL loses only 3.5% and 7.2%, respectively. This consistent gap shows that PIXEL is less sensitive to typographical perturbations despite receiving altered visual inputs. Together with the input-length results, the robustness appears to reflect two properties: avoiding typo-induced sequence fragmentation and retaining the ability to map altered visual features to useful linguistic representations.

6 Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer

After examining robustness to noisy English inputs, we turn to a different form of generalization: transferring a task learned in English to other languages. We ask whether pixel-based models transfer more effectively than text-based models and whether higher English accuracy necessarily leads to stronger crosslingual performance.

6.1 Experimental Setup

We fine-tune each model on English training data, select its checkpoint solely by English development performance, and evaluate it directly on target-language test sets. Our primary comparison is between BERT-base and PIXEL-base, whose English pretraining data are broadly comparable. We additionally include RoBERTa, PIXEL-bigrams, PIXEL-M4, mBERT, and XLM-R as reference models with different pretraining data, language coverage, and training objectives.

We focus on XNLI and PAWS-X. For XNLI, models are trained on 20,000 English MNLI examples and evaluated on German, French, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese (Conneau et al., 2018). For PAWS-X, models are trained on 49,401 English paraphrase pairs and evaluated on German, French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (Yang et al., 2019). We report English accuracy and accuracy in each target language in Table 1.99 9 Additional SIB-200 (Adelani et al., 2024) and Taxi1500 (Ma et al., 2025) results are reported in §D.

6.2 Results and Discussion

PIXEL-base transfers more effectively than BERT-base despite weaker English performance.

BERT achieves substantially higher English accuracy than PIXEL-base on both XNLI and PAWS-X, but this advantage does not carry over to the target languages. Without receiving any target-language supervision, PIXEL obtains higher target-language averages on both tasks and outperforms BERT in four of the five XNLI languages and all six PAWS-X languages (Table 1). The advantage is particularly clear for languages that share the Latin script with English: on XNLI, PIXEL exceeds BERT by 11.5 points in French and 8.6 points in Spanish. It also extends to some languages using different scripts, including Russian on XNLI and Chinese, Japanese, and Korean on PAWS-X. We attribute this broader transfer partly to the absence of a fixed subword vocabulary. BERT may fragment unfamiliar target-language words into subword sequences poorly matched to those seen during English fine-tuning, whereas PIXEL can reuse its adapted visual representations without depending on target-language vocabulary coverage.

Multilingual pretraining provides the strongest basis for crosslingual transfer.

mBERT and XLM-R achieve the highest target-language averages on both benchmarks. This is expected because large-scale multilingual pretraining improves zero-shot transfer and that stronger crosslingual representation alignment is associated with better target-language performance (Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025). Exposure to multiple languages during pretraining can place their representations in a more language-neutral space, allowing the task-specific capability learned through English fine-tuning to operate more effectively on target-language inputs. However, multilingual exposure alone seems to be insufficient. Although PIXEL-M4 includes Chinese during pretraining, it remains far behind mBERT and XLM-R on Chinese in both tasks. We attribute this gap partly to weaker adaptation: PIXEL-M4 already performs considerably worse than its multilingual counterparts on English, leaving it with a less effective task-specific capability to transfer.

7 Conclusion

We systematically examined pixel-based language models through downstream fine-tuning, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Our results identify downstream adaptation as their central practical challenge: pixel-based models require more careful optimization, longer training, and broader labelled-data coverage, suggesting that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in their pretrained representations. Once successfully adapted, however, they show greater resilience to typographical noise and stronger transfer to unseen languages than English-pretrained text-based counterparts. These findings reveal a central trade-off: removing a fixed subword vocabulary reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but places greater demands on downstream adaptation. The practical value of pixel-based models should therefore be assessed through both adaptation reliability and generalization beyond clean source-language inputs.

Limitations

We provide a systematic evaluation of downstream adaptation, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer in pixel-based models. However, we acknowledge three main limitations.

First, due to computational constraints, our experiments focus on encoder-based models and language understanding tasks. Future work could extend this evaluation to autoregressive pixel-based models and generative tasks.

Second, the evaluated pixel- and text-based models differ in architecture, pretraining data, and training objectives. Our findings therefore characterize the behavior of the tested models but do not fully isolate the causes of their differences. Controlled comparisons and mechanistic interpretability analyses could provide more direct explanations, which we leave for future work.

Finally, our fine-tuning experiments focus on learning rate, training duration, labelled-data coverage, and pretrained initialization. Other choices, including weight decay, optimization algorithms, and parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), may also affect adaptation. An exhaustive evaluation of all these dimensions is beyond our computational budget and can be explored in future work.

Appendix A Training Analysis: Settings and Supplementary Evidence

Appendix A.1 summarizes software and computing resources. The remaining sections support the three analyses in Section 4: shared settings and complete learning-rate results (Appendices A.2–A.3), warm-up and training-duration comparisons (Appendices A.4 and A.7), labelled-data coverage (Appendix A.5), and the pretraining–adaptation experiments (Appendix A.6). Appendix A.8 reports supplementary CoLA results and renderer compatibility.

A.1 Software and Computing Resources

Hardware and computational budget.

GPU experiments use NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 and RTX 4090D GPUs, with one GPU per job and up to four jobs running concurrently. The RTX 4090 has 24 GB of device memory. Available Slurm records give an estimated 527 GPU-hours for project-related training, evaluation, and exploratory experiments, including unsuccessful and interrupted runs. We calculate this estimate by summing allocated GPU counts multiplied by job durations; queued time and the original pretraining of released models are excluded. CPU-only computations and interactive allocations that cannot be attributed to the project are not included.

Software and implementation.

Table 2 lists the versions in the retained experimental environment. Historical diagnostic logs also confirm PyTorch 2.2.2 with CUDA 12.1 for the controlled BERT and PIXEL follow-ups; not every dependency version was recorded separately for earlier runs. Text-based models use Hugging Face Transformers, and pixel-based models use the PIXEL implementation (Rust et al., 2023), with the corresponding plain or bigram PangoCairo renderer. Our PIXEL checkout is based on revision 1b0da29, with local rendering changes to support bigram checkpoints and matched training/evaluation rendering. Typographical perturbations use MulTypo (Zhao et al., 2026), revision ecd72d1.

Model sizes.

Table 3 reports parameter counts computed from the checkpoint configurations. For a consistent reference, counts use a two-class prediction head at each checkpoint’s original positional capacity, excluding masked-language-model heads and the PIXEL reconstruction decoder. Task-specific label counts and position resizing introduce small differences from these reference sizes.

A.2 Shared controlled-training settings

Table 4 summarizes the controlled analyses. AdamW uses bias correction, β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}. Effective batch is minibatch size times gradient accumulation; each run uses one GPU. The LR screen uses seeds 13, 21, 42, 87, 100, 1234, 2024, 3407, 5678, and 9999. The coverage study uses seeds 42, 1234, and 5678. All training accuracies are online epoch averages collected while the model changes. Development and holdout accuracies evaluate a fixed checkpoint, with selection rules specified separately below.

A.3 Complete learning-rate results and replication checks

Tables 5–6 report every original seed, including failures, for all six LRs. Epoch-10 fit requires both online loss <1.0<1.0 and accuracy >50%>50\%. The first-fit epoch applies the same criterion at earlier epochs; a crossing followed by endpoint failure is marked separately. Holdout accuracy evaluates the best matched-selection-development checkpoint within the ten observed epochs. It can remain useful even when later training collapses. Figure 2 and the main all-seed averages retain all ten seeds at each LR.

Hardware and replication.

The 3e-5, 5e-5, 1e-5, and 1e-6 runs use RTX 4090; 4e-5 uses RTX 4090D. At 5e-6, seed 13 uses RTX 4090 and the other seeds use RTX 4090D. The original LR conditions span nodes. Same-node reruns of seeds 13, 42, and 5678 at 3e-5/5e-5 reproduce three fits versus three failures on RTX 4090D. Reruns do not replace original observations.

Matched BERT control.

BERT uses the same six LRs, ten seeds, data, optimizer settings, update counts, and selection/holdout split as PIXEL. All 60 runs use RTX 4090D, PyTorch 2.2.2+cu121, CUDA 12.1, and FP32; all fit at epoch 10. The pretrained checkpoint supplies BERT’s pooler, and only the classifier is newly initialized. Table 7 gives first-fit epochs and holdout scores.

A.4 Warm-up follow-up

Removing the 100-update warm-up gives 3/10 fits at 3e-5 and 0/10 at 5e-5. Table 8 compares 100 and 400 warm-up updates with the same ten seeds, 24k examples, batch, schedule horizon, and endpoint. New runs use one RTX 4090 node. Four baseline reruns accompany the 400-update runs; two originally failed 1e-5 seeds fit on rerun. Paired reruns match initial-head and data-order hashes, but CUDA determinism is not enforced.

Longer warm-up helps some runs and harms others: in paired reruns, seed 100 at 3e-5 improves from 33.9% to 80.9% training accuracy, while seed 21 at 1e-5 changes from fitting to failing. Among seeds fitting under both original and longer-warm-up conditions, mean holdout accuracy changes from 65.8% to 64.8% at 1e-5 and remains 65.7% at 3e-5. Extending warm-up therefore gives no consistent improvement.

A.5 Labelled coverage and generalization

Table 9 reports all fixed-15,000-update coverage runs. Within each task, the seed set, warm-up, effective batch, schedule, and development split are held fixed across sample budgets. SST-2 uses 2k/8k/24k examples and a maximum length of 64; MNLI uses 8k/24k and a maximum length of 256. The SST-2 LR differs between models (BERT 2e-5, PIXEL 3e-5), so its cross-model gap describes these model–recipe combinations. MNLI uses 2e-5 for both models. No early stopping is used.

Checkpoint selection and training fit.

We report the best recorded development accuracy on the 872-example SST-2 split or the 2,000-example matched MNLI subset. Evaluations occur at epoch boundaries after approximately 250 updates for SST-2 and 500 for MNLI. Final training accuracies in Table 9 are online epoch averages at the 15,000-update endpoint; all exceed 99.5%. The weak 24k PIXEL SST-2 seed is retained in Table 9 and the ten-seed follow-up, but excluded from the outcome-conditioned 24k point in Figure 3a. All three MNLI PIXEL seeds improve from 8k to 24k. No PAWS-X 8k/24k sample-budget experiment was run; full-data PAWS-X transfer results are a separate comparison.

Paired coverage gains.

Figure 3 plots mean development accuracy, with error bars showing the sample standard deviation of accuracy across seeds. To quantify the benefit of additional labelled examples, we subtract each seed’s smallest-budget score from its score at the larger budget before aggregation. For seed ss and sample count nn, the gain is Δs​(n)=as​(n)−as​(n0)\Delta_{s}(n)=a_{s}(n)-a_{s}(n_{0}), where n0=2​kn_{0}=2\mathrm{k} for SST-2 and 8​k8\mathrm{k} for MNLI. The annotations show mean paired gains from 2k to 8k examples on SST-2 and from 8k to 24k on MNLI, measured in percentage points. Only the PIXEL SST-2 24k point uses seeds 42 and 5678, selected after observing low development performance in seed 1234; their mean gain over 2k is 20.70 points, with a paired-gain sample SD of 0.08. This gain is conditional on these two high-generalization runs. All other points retain all three seeds. Unconditional scores and variation remain visible in Table 9.

Ten-seed SST-2 follow-up.

We retain the original three PIXEL seeds (42, 1234, 5678) and add seven distinct seeds (13, 21, 100, 2024, 3407, 777, 909) only at 24k examples. The training subset is sampled with seed 42 and remains identical across all ten runs, as does the validation split. The recipe remains LR 3e-5, 400 warm-up updates, minibatch 32 with four-step accumulation, maximum length 64, dropout 0.1, AdamW weight decay 0.01, linear decay, and 15,000 updates without early stopping. New runs use RTX 4090 GPUs across two nodes. We re-evaluate each best-development checkpoint in evaluation mode on the complete 24k training subset and the same 872 validation examples; all development scores reproduce exactly. Table 10 reports all ten runs. The ten-seed mean development accuracy is 83.20%, with sample standard deviation 7.86 points. Cross-budget comparisons use the original three paired seeds, with the outcome-conditioned 24k plotting exception described above.

Independent test evaluation.

Test scores do not enter model selection. We recover labels for 1,821 GLUE SST-2 test sentences from the authors’ public Stanford Sentiment Treebank trees, mapping root labels 0/1 to negative and 3/4 to positive and excluding neutral roots. This procedure reproduces all 872 validation labels; inference uses the original GLUE text. We test all nine original PIXEL budget checkpoints and the new low-development seed 909; six other new checkpoints remain unevaluated. At 2k/8k examples, test accuracies are 63.26/75.51% (seed 42), 65.90/77.43% (1234), and 64.69/71.77% (5678). Two normalized test sentences overlap the 24k training subset. Excluding them from every budget leaves 24k test scores of 85.10%, 65.31%, 85.82%, and 66.14% for seeds 42, 1234, 5678, and 909, preserving the findings.

A.6 Pretraining–adaptation experiments

A.6.1 SST-2 training conditions

The Random, Frozen, and Full FT comparison in Section 4.3 uses seed 42, the fixed 24k SST-2 subset, and 872 development examples. Random and Full FT train the encoder and classifier jointly, starting from random and pretrained weights, respectively. Frozen trains a linear classifier on mean-pooled representations of the fixed pretrained encoder using AdamW (LR 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 0.01, batch 256, at most 50 epochs, patience 8, no scheduler).

For Random and Full FT, BERT uses LR 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, batch 32 without accumulation, at most ten epochs, a 10% warm-up ratio, patience 3, and 128 tokens. PIXEL uses LR 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, minibatch 32 with four-step accumulation, at most 30 epochs, 100 warm-up updates, patience 8, dropout 0.1, and 64 rendered positions. Both use AdamW, weight decay 0.01, clipping at 1.0, and linear decay over their maximum-epoch horizons. Development accuracy is evaluated once per epoch, and the best-development checkpoint is reported. Patience counts evaluations without improvement. These model-specific recipes differ, and the Frozen-to-Full FT comparison also includes readout-design differences.

A.6.2 MNLI initialization intervention

We use the fixed historical 24k MNLI subset and 2,000 examples from each development split. Seeds 100 and 5678 were selected because they failed in the historical learning-rate comparison and subsequent baseline replications. We run each seed five times from each of three initializations: the original pretrained encoder, a fixed PAWS-X-adapted encoder, and a fixed Taxi1500-adapted encoder. This gives 30 runs, or ten per initialization. The target recipe uses LR 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, minibatch 32 with four-step accumulation, 100 warm-up updates for seed 100 and no warm-up for seed 5678, MSL 256, dropout 0.1, AdamW with weight decay 0.01, and clipping at 1.0. Training lasts ten epochs (1,880 updates) without early stopping, retaining the historical 80-epoch linear-decay horizon. Within each seed, the task head, target position embeddings, initial random-number states, and per-epoch data order are identical across the three initializations. Only non-position encoder weights are transferred; source classifiers, poolers, and optimizer states are discarded.

The PAWS-X source uses 49,401 English training examples; its checkpoint is selected at epoch 3 with 89.3% source-development accuracy. The Taxi1500 source uses 860 English training examples and 106 development examples across six classes; its checkpoint is selected at epoch 55 with development macro-F1 0.541. Neither source is selected using MNLI outcomes. Source training and checkpoint-selection data show no normalized sentence overlap with the target training or evaluated development subsets under the current loaders. The historical target subset has 29 sentence overlaps with the complete official development data; we retain its unchanged partition for the paired comparison. Source supervision and computation differ between initializations.

For seed 100, the first repeat uses different RTX 4090 nodes for the original and adapted runs; repeats 2–5 run the three initializations sequentially in the same GPU allocation. All seed-5678 runs use RTX 4090D GPUs on one node, in separate allocations. All available paired configuration audits pass. CUDA determinism is not enforced, so matching seeds and initialization states does not guarantee identical executions. Figure 4b–c and Table 11 retain all repeats, including seed 100’s first repeat with its node difference and the failed Taxi1500 run for seed 5678.

Original initialization succeeds in 1/10 runs overall, compared with 10/10 for PAWS-X and 9/10 for Taxi1500. The successful original run first meets the training-fit criterion at epoch 6; successful adapted runs meet it at epoch 1 or 2. Because the two seeds were selected from previously observed failures, these repeated executions characterize the effect of initialization on failure-prone settings and do not estimate PIXEL’s overall failure rate. The intervention changes encoder initialization and supports an adaptation-gap explanation; it does not isolate the pretraining objective or decoder removal as the cause.

A.7 Longer-budget MNLI comparison

This comparison supports the training-duration analysis in Section 4.1. It uses 24,000 training examples, 2,000 examples from each development split, maximum sequence length 256, and the same ten seeds for both models. Within each model, only the seed changes. PIXEL-base uses minibatch 32 with four-step accumulation, LR 10−510^{-5}, up to 80 epochs, 400 warm-up updates, and patience 12. BERT uses batch 32, LR 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, up to ten epochs, a 10% warm-up ratio, and patience 3. These model-specific recipes differ from the controlled ten-epoch LR screen.

Table 12 reports the best matched-development checkpoint for every seed. Seven PIXEL runs exceed 45% development accuracy; their best-checkpoint epochs have a median of 21, compared with 3 for BERT on the same seven seeds. The three near-chance PIXEL runs remain in the table but are excluded from this paired duration summary. This historical development-based selection is distinct from the epoch-10 training criterion in the LR screen. Best-checkpoint epoch measures when development performance peaks, not the total number of epochs executed.

A.8 CoLA results and renderer compatibility

CoLA.

Changing maximum sequence length from 196 to 64 changes PIXEL-base MCC from 0.103 to 0.188 and PIXEL-M4 MCC from 0.228 to 0.172. The mixed directions show that shorter rendered sequences do not consistently improve performance. These supplementary configuration checks are separate from the controlled MNLI and SST-2 analyses.

Renderer compatibility.

Plain and bigram renderers produce different patch sequences, so training and evaluation must use the renderer matched to the checkpoint. An early evaluation path used a mismatched renderer for bigram checkpoints. After correction, clean evaluation scores agreed with the saved checkpoint scores to within 0.0001. All final reported results use matched renderers.

Appendix B Dataset Details

SST-2.

This binary movie-review sentiment task supplies the English clean-task and typo-robustness comparisons. The controlled supervision analysis uses fixed, stratified subsets of 2,000, 8,000, and 24,000 labelled examples, three seeds, and the same 872-example development split; the metric is accuracy.

MNLI.

This three-class entailment task contains premise–hypothesis pairs from multiple genres. The learning-rate analysis uses 24,000 training examples, a 2,000-example matched development selection subset, and separate matched and mismatched holdouts of 2,000 examples each. The supervision analysis compares 8,000 and 24,000 examples. We report accuracy.

CoLA.

This English grammatical-acceptability task is a supplementary fine-tuning case, not a primary typographical-robustness finding. Its binary labels are evaluated by Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). The available configuration checks and weak PIXEL outcomes are described in §A.8.

XNLI.

We fine-tune on 20,000 English MNLI examples and evaluate zero-shot on German, French, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese. The source and target tasks use the same three inference labels. Table 1 reports accuracy for English and each target language; the target average excludes English.

PAWS-X.

This binary paraphrase-identification task contains high-overlap sentence pairs for which lexical similarity alone need not determine the label. We fine-tune on 49,401 English pairs and evaluate zero-shot on German, French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. We report accuracy and average only the target languages.

SIB-200.

This seven-class multilingual topic task provides 701 English training examples, 99 English development examples, and 204 test examples per evaluated language. We evaluate German, French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, and Korean after English-only fine-tuning and report macro F1 in Table 14.

Taxi1500.

This six-class topic task is constructed from Bible text. Our English source split has 860 training examples. We evaluate German, French, Russian, and Chinese without target-language supervision and report accuracy in Table 15. Weak English source-task scores for some PIXEL checkpoints limit transfer interpretation.

Appendix C Robustness: Settings and Complete Results

The SST-2 and MNLI robustness evaluations use checkpoints selected on clean English development data after fine-tuning on fixed 24,000-example clean subsets. Each selected checkpoint is evaluated on the same clean held-out examples and their MulTypo perturbations at 5%, 10%, 20%, and 40% noise; no noisy examples are used for additional training. The figure reports relative accuracy loss and the percentage change in mean input length relative to clean inputs. Table 13 gives absolute accuracy for all eight evaluated models; the small change of a near-floor model should not be interpreted as useful robustness.

Appendix D Additional Cross-Lingual Transfer Results

SIB-200 and Taxi1500 have much smaller English training splits than XNLI and PAWS-X. Their source-task limitations make them supporting cases rather than evidence for the principal transfer comparison in §6. The per-language scores below retain weak English checkpoints rather than selecting only successful models.
